power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The discovery of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) has revealed a conceptual inconsistency at the heart of disorders of consciousness (DoC) nosology.

Advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that behavioral unresponsiveness does not necessarily imply the absence of consciousness or cognitive capacity, yet contemporary diagnostic categories continue equating unresponsiveness with unconsciousness.

This equivalence is embedded throughout DoC nomenclature, where behavioral syndromes such as the vegetative state (VS) and minimally conscious state (MCS) are defined by what patients are inferred to experience (i.e., their state of mind) but operationalized on the basis of what they are observed to do (or not do).
We argue that this category error now impedes the translation of over two decades of scientific advances into a coherent clinical framework.

First, it has fostered the widespread but incorrect conflation of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), despite the fact that the two concepts identify different patient populations and may carry distinct implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.
Second, it renders contemporary DoC nosology incapable of coherently incorporating modern neuroimaging and electrophysiological findings.
Because the absence of consciousness is an entrenched, definitional component of the VS, its behavioral phenotype cannot be reconciled with covert neurophysiological phenotypes such as CC and CMD.

As a result, current nomenclature impedes the development of a phenotype-endotype framework in which bedside behavioral classifications are complemented by biologically informed categories derived from advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological assessments.
We trace the origins of this problem to a historical shift whereby the definitions of VS and MCS evolved from descriptions of observable behavior into claims about a patient's mental state.

Disentangling responsiveness from consciousness, we argue, is essential if the field is to incorporate contemporary evidence and develop a coherent, biologically informed nosology of DoC, which, in our view, is best pursued within a phenotype-endotype framework.

There is now abundant evidence that a substantial proportion of brain injury survivors who do not immediately recover may harbor a level of consciousness and cognitive function that far exceeds what can be detected in conventional, behavior-based clinical assessments. [1] [2] [3] [4] This evidence has revolutionized our understanding of the assessment of disorders of consciousness (DoC) 5, 6 such as coma, the vegetative state (VS, also referred to as Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome), and the minimally conscious state (MCS), and has been instrumental in promoting an agenda of evidence-based competency in managing these conditions that is now codified in international guidelines. 7, 8 Nonetheless, this evidence has generated substantial confusion with respect to the interpretation and implication of such results with respect to the nosology of DoC, 9 something that can have complex consequences for patients and other stakeholders.

text.text: Several terms have been proposed to describe patients whose level of awareness or cognitive capacity exceeds what is detectable at the bedside, such as covert awareness (CA), 10, 11 covert consciousness (CC), 12, 13 or cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), 14 among others. 9 Rather than representing isolated terminological disputes, we argue that the challenges raised by these labels reflect a deeper conceptual problem within contemporary DoC nosology: the tendency to define diagnostic categories by what patients are inferred to experience (i.e., their state of mind) rather than by the behavior on which that inference rests.

text.text: As a result, current diagnostic frameworks obscure important distinctions among emerging neuroimaging and electrophysiological findings and hinder their integration into a coherent clinical framework.
This category error has at least two important consequences for the field.
First, we highlight the common but incorrect practice of using the labels Covert Consciousness/Covert Awareness and Cognitive Motor Dissociation interchangeably.

This conflation is both erroneous, because the two categories of terms do not identify the same subset of DoC patients (i.e., are not coextensive), and unwanted, because it robs the field of an important opportunity for developing novel assessments and patient-tailored interventions.

Second, we discuss the complex yet paramount challenge of accommodating novel concepts, such as CC, CA, and CMD, within a coherent and modern DoC nomenclature and evaluate the advantages and difficulties of two possible frameworks that achieve this goal.
Finally, we trace both issues to a common historical origin: the gradual redefinition of the notion of VS (and MCS) from a behavioral description into an inference about a patient's state of mind.

While this historical shift is, as we discuss, the root of both issues, in what follows we deliberately begin by distinguishing CC and CMD because this is likely to be the most consequential and immediately actionable issue for current practice.

The ensuing nosological discussion, on the other hand, shows how this distinction forces the field to make a decision as to the best path forward, and the historical analysis explains how the field has come to need such a decision.

A brief history of covert awareness, covert consciousness, and cognitive motor dissociation Since the landmark case published in 2006 by Owen and colleagues, 16 several names have been used to refer to the phenomenon whereby the extent of a patient's responsiveness at the bedside, typically evaluated with neurobehavioral protocols such as the Coma Recovery Scale Revised (CRS-R), 17 is exceeded by what they demonstrate through advanced, task-based, imaging and electrophysiology assessments. i The names used to refer to this include CA, 10, 11 CC, 12, 13 CMD, 14 along with some now less used terms, such as functional locked in syndrome (fLIS) 18 and "non-behavioral" minimally conscious state, 19 among others. 9 While being a measure of the rapid development of this field, such panoply of names is generating confusion concerning the exact subset of patients each picks out (i.e., what is the exact definition of each label) and how such terms ought to be integrated in a modern DoC nosology, limiting opportunities for further understanding of these conditions.

text.text: The clearest instance of such confusion is the fact that the term CA is often used interchangeably with the term CMD. 3, [20] [21] [22] This, we argue, is a harmful and factually incorrect conflation of terms.

text.text: The term 'Cognitive Motor Dissociation,' on the other hand, was proposed to operationally identify patients who are behaviorally in VS or MCS minus (MCS-; meaning they can exhibit subtle non-reflexive behaviors, such as tracking, indicative of the presence of awareness 29 ) and covertly demonstrate the ability to follow commands through active (i.e., task-based) imaging or electrophysiology. 14, 30 CMD may reflect an underlying disconnection between thalamus and motor cortex. 31 These patients demonstrate a residual neurocognitive capacity meeting, at a minimum, criteria for MCS "plus" (MCS+; which describes a patient who can demonstrate response to command 29 ) despite their behavioral presentation.

text.text: Despite describing different phenomena, the terms CC and CMD are now often taken to be synonymous, 3, [20] [21] [22] possibly as a symptom of the fact that, in the absence of a means to objectively measure consciousness in an individual, we pragmatically rely on voluntary behavior as a proxy for its presence. 5, 32 There are at least two reasons for this conflation.

text.text: First, CC and CMD have been, in practice, operationalized in the same manner (i.e., a positive response to an active AIE paradigm), so that the two labels have had no occasion to come apart.

Second, a behaviorally unresponsive patient who is nonetheless conscious calls for an explanation of the phenomenon, which is exactly what the CMD proposal provides: a dissociation between the cognitive systems that initiate willful action and the motor system that executes it. 31 Yet, conflating these two terms is both incorrect and undesirable.

text.text: For, if a patient can demonstrate behaviorally that they are conscious (i.e., MCS-), it makes little sense, should they also be able to respond to verbal commands as detected with fMRI or EEG, to refer to them as being covertly conscious.
An MCS patient is, by definition, overtly conscious, no matter how subtle the behavioral signs of awareness might be.

Thus, referring to such a patient as covertly conscious is as much a contradictio in terminis as was the rightfully deprecated term coma vigil. 33 In other words, CMD implies the presence of consciousness.

text.text: Where that consciousness is not behaviorally manifest (i.e., patients meeting the behavioral criteria for coma or VS), CMD must therefore also imply CC.
However, where the presence of consciousness is already overt (i.e., patients meeting the behavioral definition of MCS-), the CC label would be contradictory and does not apply (cf.

text.text: Notably, the Curing Coma Campaign's working group on CMD reached the same conclusion: while adopting the original operational definition of CMD, it noted that, although the two concepts overlap, covert awareness and CMD apply to different subsets of patients, the former being restricted, by definition, to behaviorally unresponsive patients and the latter extending to patients in MCS-.

The group also noted that a patient may be aware yet fail to meet the definition of CMD. 30 In addition, foregoing the distinction between CC and CMD is undesirable for the field because it fails to recognize the fact that a patient might well be covertly conscious while being unable to meet the definition of CMD.

text.text: It is perfectly possible for a patient to be conscious but unable to demonstrate so via active MRI/EEG tasks due to the multiple cognitive processes that must be intact and operate in concert to complete the tasks. 5, 34 As originally discussed by Owen and colleagues, 34 active 27 (e.g., "motor imagery") tasks are very cognitively demanding, requiring sustained allocation of executive attention, working memory, intention, and rule-based decisionmaking. 1, 32 Yet, patients with a DoC are very likely to have, with high prevalence, sensory, attentional, and linguistic impairments, 35, 36 and, even where such processes are intact, they might still have insufficient arousal regulation which would prevent them from performing cognitively demanding tasks over the long durations required for AIE assessments. 37 Unsurprisingly, active paradigms are well known to suffer from low sensitivity to a state of consciousness, 5, 27 with only 38% of patients who follow commands behaviorally generating a response to task-based MRI or EEG. 1 Failing to distinguish between CC and CMD thus robs the field of the opportunity to develop approaches that can detect the presence of a state of consciousness in the absence of both overt and covert response to command.

text.text: Retaining the distinction between the two monikers also recognizes that they address separate, if confounded, issues.
CMD refers to a capacity: the possibility that someone might have a motor-system-related impairment masking the real extent of their residual cognitive functions.
CC refers to whether a given patient possesses a state of awareness (what is sometimes referred to as 'creature consciousness' 54 ), whether it feels like something 28 to be them.

text.text: The second major issue raised by CMD and CC is one of nosology.
How should we classify a patient who fulfills the behavioral criteria for VS, yet demonstrates command-following through neuroimaging?

At first glance, the answer seems obvious: following the logic of conventional neurobehavioral assessments, detection of command-following is indicative of (at least) MCS+, so the patient should be classified accordingly.
Nonetheless, the standard DoC nomenclature is anchored in readily apparent levels of behavioral responsiveness.

The emergence of AIEs therefore raises a broader question: should diagnostic categories originally defined by overt behavior be extended to include evidence of awareness derived from brain activity alone?

The Curing Coma Campaign has explicitly left this question open, noting that forthcoming mechanistic, epidemiological, and outcome data "will determine whether the nosology of DoC requires modification." 30 Broadly speaking, there appear to be at least two approaches to answering this question which, most crucially, differ in what each proposes to serve as the primary classifier: the observable behavioral phenotype versus the inferred level of consciousness.

text.text: A framework of this kind is also the natural home for the proposal to organize DoC classification around cognitive capacities, whether probed overtly or covertly. 66 In ACCESS, for example, the 'cognitive content' item of the AVCM score is rated on a single scale, from none to complex cognition, whatever the source of the evidence (i.e., clinical examination, task-based AIE).

text.text: Cognitive capacities are precisely the kind of endotype such a framework is meant to capture, and keeping them distinct from the behavioral phenotype is what allows a covertly demonstrated capacity to be recorded without re-labelling the patient's behavioral state.

In addition, this is also where the distinction drawn above between the question of whether a patient is conscious (i.e., creature-consciousness) and what their consciousness contains (i.e., conscious contents) pays off: the former is captured by the CC designation, whereas the capacities and contents a patient's consciousness comprises are captured by the cognitive endotypes, with the added benefit of allowing the field to pursue this understudied issue 55, 66, 67 without disturbing the answer to the first question.

This immediately highlights a critical issue with applying a phenotype-endotype approach to the existing DoC nosology: by the most recent international guidelines iii , VS is defined as a "state of wakefulness without awareness" 68 whereby patients "are therefore considered unaware of themselves and their surroundings" 8 due to the presence of "[s]pontaneous eye-opening signaling wakefulness, but [absence of] evidence of purposeful behavior suggesting awareness of self or environment". 7 In light of these definitions, it becomes inescapably contradictory to characterize a patient as being both unaware of themselves and their surrounding (i.e., VS) and, at once, capable of intentionally modulating their brain activity in response to command (i.e., CMD).

Given the associations that have accrued to the terms VS, UWS (as discussed below), and MCS, it is not easy to imagine them amenable to this phenotype-endotype approach.

Perhaps, the field could consider replacing the conventional diagnostic labels with novel ones that describe the clinically observable phenomena key to the DoC diagnosis: wakefulness and responsiveness.

A coma patient might, for example, be described as unarousable (i.e., without eye opening, spontaneous or stimulus-induced) and limited to reflexive responses, whereas a VS patient could be described as wakeful albeit behaviorally reflexive.
An MCS patient, instead, could be described as wakeful and behaviorally intentional without (i.e., MCS-) or with intact basic language function (i.e., MCS+).

A nomenclature as in this example would be in the spirit of the AVCM score, 65 whose arousal and volition dimensions characterize what is observed at the bedside without committing to an inference about awareness (although it is notable that ACCESS itself retains VS/UWS and MCS as its clinical phenotypes, thus inheriting the tension discussed above).

text.text: Importantly, under such a nomenclature, it would no longer be problematic to describe a patient as having an unarousable reflexive (i.e., coma) or wakeful reflexive (i.e., VS) phenotype and a Covert Consciousness or Cognitive Motor Dissociation endotype.

An alternative to the phenotype-endotype approach is to retain the standard DoC nomenclature and focus diagnosis on the detection of level of consciousness, an approach that seems implicit in the 2020 EU guidelines for the diagnosis of coma and other DoC. 8 In this approach, each novel AIE test is just another item in an extended, multimodal, assessment in which "a given patient should be diagnosed with the highest level of consciousness as revealed by any of the […] approaches (clinical, EEG, neuroimaging)". 8 The consciousness-first approach recognizes that the almost totality of novel AIEs developed for DoC have been focused on the important question of detecting the presence of consciousness in patients whose behavior is not sufficient to demonstrate it. 69 In this approach, then, the hypothetical patient described at the beginning of this section (classified as "VS with CMD" under the phenotype-endotype approach) would be considered, simply, MCS.

text.text: As advantageous as it might seem to accommodate CMD and CC within the traditional DoC categories, doing so would make the patient's phenotype dependent on an endotype that is challenging to obtain, not yet validated or standardized, and of unknown upper limit.

For, 20 years after the first reported case, AIEs remain in a state of endorsement without implementation, 70 with very few clinicians worldwide having access to such techniques. 71 While this limitation is practical and may well prove temporary, two others would remain even if access were universal.

text.text: First, considering the characteristically fluctuating responsiveness of DoC patients 72 and that misdiagnosis rates are known to decrease dramatically when assessments are repeated, 73 a phenotype that hinges on a single AIE result (given AIE assessments are rarely repeated) would be significantly more fragile than one based on serial bedside assessment.

text.text: Second, and most importantly, behavioral and AIE-based categories constrain a patient's capacities from opposite sides.
A behavioral diagnosis of MCS carries a floor as well as a ceiling: it implies the presence of some intentional behavior and the absence of behaviors indicating emergence, respectively.

A positive active paradigm, on the other hand, only establishes a floor, command following and hence capacities at least at the level of MCS+, with no upper limit on what else the patient may be capable of.

While any label can underestimate a patient's capacities, the specific problem with relabeling such a patient as just MCS is that it asserts an upper limit (i.e., absence of evidence of emergence) not supported by the evidence, by importing a category with a ceiling (i.e., behaviorally defined MCS) onto evidence that has none (i.e., AIE defined MCS).

A label such as 'VS with CMD', on the other hand, asserts no such limit: the phenotype records what was observed at the bedside and the endotype what was demonstrated by other means, and neither bounds the other.

In addition, the consciousness-first approach is challenged by the finding that AIEs can reveal clinically important information also in patients who are behaviorally in MCS. 25 This is telling: if the value of an AIE result were truly exhausted by its raising a patient's diagnosed level of consciousness, a positive result in a patient known to be (behaviorally) in MCS would have to carry no information.

text.text: Yet initial data suggest that MCSpatients with CMD improve on the CRS-R at 3 months at substantially higher rates than MCSpatients without CMD. 25 Failing to distinguish between phenotype and endotype also risks antagonizing the basic promise of a more granular understanding of DoC, a more patient-tailored categorization, and a precision medicine approach to prognosis and intervention selection. 64, 65 Weighing the two approaches, we favor the phenotype-endotype framework.

text.text: While what we described here should be seen as an example of how such an approach could work, we do argue that a framework in which bedside behavioral categories describe what is observed, while advanced imaging and electrophysiology define endotypes that qualify, rather than overwrite, those descriptions, 65 is the one most likely to deliver to DoC the benefits that other areas of medicine have derived from similar schemes: 57-64 a more granular characterization of patients, testable hypotheses about the prognostic and therapeutic significance of each endotype, and a path toward precision medicine that does not require first settling what consciousness is and how best to measure it.

text.text: Three clarifications are in order.
First, the advantage of the phenotype-endotype framework does not lie in how many distinctions it draws.

Either approach can be kept coarse or made fine: a consciousness-first scheme could stop at conscious versus unconscious or subdivide consciousness into levels and dimensions, just as a phenotype-endotype scheme could stop at four bedside categories or subdivide each by endotype (e.g., VS with CMD, VS with PCI>PCI*, VS with neither observed, VS with neither tested).

text.text: The advantage lies in what the additional distinctions are anchored to (i.e., observed behavior and measured biology rather than an inferred state), and in the fact that they can be added only as the evidence warrants, as biomarkers prove prognostically or therapeutically informative.

Second, the framework takes no stand on whether the boundary between reflexive and intentional behavior also marks a boundary in consciousness itself, as some have questioned. 66 Rather, it uses that boundary as a phenotype and as an evidential threshold, not as a claim about awareness.

text.text: Third, any such scheme must serve families, clinicians, researchers and ethicists, who read labels differently and require different things from them. 30, 56 This might favor an architecture in which a stable, descriptive bedside phenotype can be communicated in plain language, while the endotype layer carries the technical qualifications that clinicians and researchers need, and it is also where a plain-language umbrella term such as 'covert consciousness', as proposed previously, 56 can do its work without erasing the distinctions beneath it.

text.text: Given the transformative advances that the DoC field has witnessed over the last few decades, how did the notion of a VS come to be defined by an inferred state of mind as opposed to clinically observable behavior?
When Jennett and Plum coined the term vegetative state in 1972, they were careful about the epistemological limits of their proposal.

For, they explicitly noted that the name should not imply more than is known, and that the clinical syndrome "describes behaviour." 15 They also acknowledged that, in these patients, the inference from behavior to the presence or absence of conscious experience is uncertain, noting that one can only "infer the presence or absence of conscious experience in another person." 15 Importantly, their caution was thus not the generic observation that all minds other than our own are known only by inference (i.e., the problem of other minds), but the specific one that in these patients it is unclear whether the inference to the absence of awareness is warranted, and that it should therefore not be written into the name.

text.text: It was over 20 years later, that the Multi-Society Task Force on the Persistent VS redefined the vegetative state as "a clinical condition of complete unawareness of the self and the environment" (emphasis added), 74 despite recognizing that Jennett and Plum described it as a "state of wakefulness without detectable awareness."

text.text: While the diagnostic criteria set by the Task Force were behavioral in nature (e.g., no evidence of purposeful behavior), the definition itself equated behavioral phenotype (i.e., unresponsiveness) with mental state (i.e., unawareness), something which they reasoned was supported by multiple lines of evidence. 75 Although the Task Force overtly grappled with the limitations tied to the inferential nature of the definition, they nonetheless concluded that VS patients "are noncognitive, nonsentient, and incapable of conscious experience" 74 (emphasis added).

text.text: The inferential nature of the VS diagnosis was already established in the field even before the Task Force codified it.

In 1992, for example, a member of the Multi-Society Task Force acknowledged that "our only means of ascertainment of another person's cognition and awareness is by inference," and specifically raised the possibility of false-positive VS diagnostic error, that a patient "could retain a rudimentary level of awareness that our crude tests cannot detect." 76 Yet, foreshadowing the 1994 guidelines, this issue was considered as an irreducible epistemic limitation to be managed, not as a reason to reconsider the VS definition.

text.text: Although a seemingly subtle change, by 1994, the inference had become the definition.

The following year, the American Academy of Neurology also codified this same definition by stating that "[t]he vegetative state is a clinical condition of complete unawareness of the self and the environment" 77 (emphasis added).
While, again, behavioral criteria were offered as the means of diagnosis, what was being diagnosed is a state of unawareness.

To be clear, the problem here is that in the case of VS specifically, the inference from unresponsiveness to unconsciousness is invalid (i.e., is based on interpreting absence of evidence of awareness as evidence of its absence), 32 as demonstrated empirically, 1, 78 and yet it has come to be the very definition of the category.

text.text: In this sense, the same concern does not apply to positive inferences drawn from overt or covert responses which, when detected, imply the presence of a state of awareness (assuming one agrees that the demonstrated behavior is of the kind that licenses such inference; e.g., willful responses).
This connotation of the term Vegetative State, defined by the absence of awareness, has never left the field since the Task Force's work.

Indeed, by 2002, the Aspen criteria had fully absorbed it and distinguished MCS from VS on the basis of "partial preservation of conscious awareness." 79 Although, again, it is recognized that the diagnostic separator between the two categories is the presence of behaviors associated with conscious awareness, what is being diagnosed is the state of absence of consciousness (cf., Ref 79 , Table 1, p. 350).

text.text: This connotation, however, did not go unnoticed.

In 2010, Laureys and colleagues proposed renaming the condition as Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS), explicitly choosing 'the clinically descriptive term unresponsive rather than the misleading unaware'. 33 While we share the spirit of this proposal, the definition of UWS remains the same as that of VS (i.e., wakefulness in the absence of awareness), making our criticism equally applicable to the new label.

text.text: Indeed, none of the recent guidelines suggests UWS as the recommended label.

Rather, the new term is either rejected outright 68 or simply appended to the VS abbreviation (i.e., VS/UWS), while retaining 'wakefulness without awareness' as the definition for both. 7, 8 Furthermore, as discussed elsewhere, 68, [80] [81] [82] the label "unresponsive" is incorrect at the bedside (i.e., UWS patients do show responses, albeit at a reflex level 68 ) and in light of the AIE evidence (i.e., some UWS patients can respond in active tasks 1, 4 ) which renders the name less diagnostically precise. 81 Indeed, the only sense in which the label is accurate is when read, as intended, 33 as the absence of any behavioral response that evidences awareness, which is exactly the inference-laden content the label was supposed to shed.

text.text: Thus, while superficially appealing, UWS simply shifted the inference from 'unaware' into 'unresponsive' without removing it.

Most importantly, the relabeling does not touch the problem at issue here; that is, 'UWS with CMD' is as much a contradiction in terms as is 'VS with CMD', the former denying the response, the latter denying awareness.

Another 30 years since the Task Force's landmark work, the most recent guidelines 7, 8, 68, 83 still suffer from the deep echoes of the equation of unresponsiveness with unconsciousness, framing the diagnostic process as a search for evidence of a patient's state of (un)awareness.

text.text: To be clear, our aim is not to rehabilitate 'vegetative state' as a behavioral label, but to insist that whatever label is used denote a behavioral phenotype and not an inferred state of mind.
Two important corollaries emerge from this renewed understanding.

First, one might also question whether the term Minimally Conscious State suffers from an analogous shortcoming and should be changed to something closer to the original Minimally Responsive State (MIN-R) 85, 86 label suggested by the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine (ACRM) in 1995 as "a descriptive term that refers to patients who are no longer comatose or vegetative" (emphasis added) and whose behavioral "responses are inconsistent but indicative of meaningful interaction with the environment." 87 Alternatively, in an effort to make the label more precise and transparent a term to the effect of Minimal Non-Reflexive Responsiveness could be adopted.

Second, behavioral scales such as the CRS-R 17 are often interpreted in a graded fashion with "[h]igher CRS-R scores representing higher levels of consciousness". 88, 89 Yet, while certain threshold behaviors pragmatically justify inferring the presence (versus absence) of consciousness, interpreting progressively higher CRS-R scores as reflecting progressively higher levels of consciousness is another manifestation of the incorrect equation of behavior with state of mind.

text.text: While the CRS-R was explicitly developed around a hierarchical model of increasingly complex neurobehavioral responses, and substantial psychometric evidence supports its validity, 90 whether progression along this hierarchy should be interpreted as reflecting progressively higher levels of consciousness remains unclear. 67 Higher CRS-R scores are thus better understood as strengthening the evidence that a patient is conscious at all (i.e., creature consciousness), and hence the probability that consciousness is present, rather than as quantifying its level.

text.text: Similarly, higher scores also document a wider repertoire of behaviors and, plausibly, of conscious contents and capacities.
Neither reading, however, licenses treating the score as a quantity of consciousness: the CRS-R is an evidential scale, not a consciousness scale.
How to unwind such deeply embedded associations across specialists and the general public alike is a key challenge.

Yet unless this distinction is made, the field risks continuing to mistake evidence of consciousness for consciousness itself, obscuring the interpretation of emerging biomarkers and hindering the development of a modern precision-medicine framework for disorders of consciousness.
In the meantime, two steps are available now.

The first is to stop using covert consciousness and cognitive motor dissociation interchangeably, reserving the former for the presence of awareness in behaviorally unresponsive patients and the latter for covert command-following, whatever the behavioral phenotype.

The second is for the field to start discussing what labels would best fit a phenotype-endotype nosology in which bedside categories describe what is observed, while advanced imaging and electrophysiology evidence defines endotypes that qualify, rather than overwrite, them.
